SCI.q: A student pours 200 g of water into a cup and stirs in 20 g of salt until it dissolves. What is the mass of the salt water?
a: This subtracts the salt. The salt didn't leave the cup, so its mass is still counted.
This counts only the water. Dissolved salt is invisible, but it is still there and still has mass.
Mass is conserved: 200 g + 20 g = 220 g. Dissolving doesn't destroy any matter.
This adds 20 g twice. Nothing new was added, so the total is 200 g + 20 g.

SCI.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
a: An ice cube melting
Melting is a physical change. The water is still water, just in liquid form.
An iron nail rusting
Rust is a new substance formed when iron reacts with oxygen and water. That makes it a chemical change.
Paper being cut in half
Cutting changes size and shape only. Each piece is still paper, so this is a physical change.
Sugar dissolving in tea
Dissolving is a physical change. The sugar is still sugar and could be recovered by evaporating the water.

SCI.q: Baking soda and vinegar are sealed in a plastic bag. The bag has a mass of 150 g. The mixture fizzes and the bag puffs up. What is the mass of the sealed bag now?
a: Less than 150 g
Mass would go down only if gas escaped. The bag is sealed, so the gas is trapped inside.
Exactly 150 g
In a closed system, mass is conserved. The gas is new, but it is made from matter already in the bag.
More than 150 g
No matter entered the sealed bag. Puffing up means more volume, not more mass.
It cannot be measured
You can measure it on a scale. The sealed bag will still read 150 g.

SCI.q: A 30 g ice cube melts completely in a closed container. What is the mass of the water?
a: Melting doesn't cut matter in half. Changing state doesn't change mass.
No water escaped from the closed container, so no mass was lost.
Melting is a physical change. The water has the same mass as the ice did.
Nothing was added. Liquid water has the same mass as the ice it came from.

SCI.q: Which mixture could be separated most easily using a magnet?
a: Salt and water
Salt is not magnetic. Evaporation would separate this mixture.
Sand and iron filings
Iron is magnetic. A magnet pulls the filings out and leaves the sand behind.
Sugar and flour
Neither is magnetic. A magnet would not pull either one out.
Rice and beans
Neither is magnetic. You could sort these by hand or with a sieve.

SCI.q: Which observation is the BEST evidence that a new substance formed?
a: Water turns to steam when heated
Steam is still water in gas form. This is a physical change.
Clay is rolled into a ball
Only the shape changed. The clay is still clay.
Two liquids are mixed, bubbles form, and the cup gets warm
A gas forming and a temperature change are signs of a chemical change, which makes a new substance.
Juice is poured into a taller glass
The juice only changed containers. Its substance didn't change.

SCI.q: Which property tells how much space an object takes up?
a: Mass
Mass is the amount of matter in an object, not the space it fills.
Volume
Volume is the amount of space an object takes up.
Color
Color is a property you can see. It doesn't tell how much space something fills.
Temperature
Temperature tells how hot or cold something is, not its size.

SCI.q: Which substance will dissolve in water?
a: Sand
Sand sinks to the bottom and stays visible. It doesn't dissolve.
Pebbles
Pebbles don't break apart and spread through the water, so they don't dissolve.
Cooking oil
Oil floats on top of water in a layer. It doesn't dissolve.
Sugar
Sugar spreads evenly through the water and disappears from view. It dissolves and forms a solution.

SCI.q: A ball is thrown straight up into the air. Why does it fall back to the ground?
a: Friction pulls it down
Friction slows objects that rub together. It doesn't pull things toward Earth.
Gravity pulls it toward Earth
Gravity is the force that pulls objects toward the center of Earth.
Air pushes it down
Air resistance slows the ball, but it doesn't cause the fall.
It runs out of energy and stops
Objects don't just stop. A force, gravity, changes the ball's motion and pulls it down.

SCI.q: A car travels 120 miles in 2 hours at a steady speed. What is its speed?
a: 30 miles per hour
This divides by 4 instead of 2. Speed = 120 ÷ 2.
60 miles per hour
Speed = distance ÷ time. 120 miles ÷ 2 hours = 60 miles per hour.
118 miles per hour
This subtracts instead of dividing. Speed means distance divided by time.
240 miles per hour
This multiplies instead of dividing. Speed = distance ÷ time.

SCI.q: Two students push identical toy cars on the same floor. Kim pushes much harder than Leo. What most likely happens?
a: Both cars travel the same distance
The forces are different, so the changes in motion will be different too.
Leo's car travels farther
Leo used the smaller force. A smaller push makes a smaller change in motion.
Kim's car moves faster and farther
A greater force causes a greater change in motion, so Kim's car speeds up more and goes farther.
Neither car moves
Both students push the cars, so both cars move.

SCI.q: A toy car rolls off a ramp onto four different surfaces. On which surface will it stop the soonest?
a: Smooth tile
Tile is smooth, so it has low friction. The car would roll a long way.
Ice
Ice has very little friction. The car would roll the farthest.
Wood floor
Wood is fairly smooth. The car would roll farther than on carpet.
Thick carpet
Carpet is rough, so it creates the most friction and slows the car fastest.

SCI.q: Two teams pull on a rope with equal force in a tug-of-war. What happens to the rope?
a: It moves toward the stronger team
Neither team is stronger here. The forces are equal.
It moves up into the air
The pulls are sideways. Nothing is pulling the rope upward.
It does not move
Equal forces in opposite directions are balanced. Balanced forces don't change motion.
It speeds up
Only unbalanced forces make an object speed up.

SCI.q: A soccer ball is sitting still on the grass. What will make it start moving?
a: An unbalanced force, like a kick
An unbalanced force changes an object's motion. A kick starts the ball moving.
Balanced forces acting on it
Balanced forces cancel out. The ball would stay still.
Gravity alone
Gravity pulls the ball down into the ground. It doesn't roll the ball across flat grass.
Nothing can make it move
Any unbalanced force, like a push or a kick, can start it moving.

SCI.q: In the food chain grass → rabbit → fox, where does the energy first come from?
a: The soil
Soil gives plants water and nutrients, but not the energy they use to make food.
The sun
Grass uses sunlight to make food. That energy then passes to the rabbit and the fox.
The rabbit
The rabbit gets its energy by eating grass, so it isn't the first source.
The fox
The fox is at the end of the chain. It gets energy from the rabbit.

SCI.q: What is the main job of decomposers like mushrooms and bacteria?
a: Make food from sunlight
That is what producers, like plants, do.
Hunt other animals
That is what predators do.
Break down dead things and return nutrients to the soil
Decomposers recycle nutrients from dead plants and animals so producers can use them again.
Pollinate flowers
Bees and other pollinators do that job, not decomposers.

SCI.q: In a field, snakes eat mice. If all the snakes were removed, what would most likely happen to the mice at first?
a: The mouse population would increase
With no predators eating them, more mice survive, so their population grows at first.
The mouse population would decrease
The mice lost a predator, not a food source, so their numbers would go up.
The mice would become producers
Mice are consumers. They can't make their own food from sunlight.
Nothing would change
Removing a predator affects the whole food web, starting with its prey.

SCI.q: Which organism is a producer?
a: Hawk
A hawk eats other animals. It is a consumer.
Oak tree
Plants make their own food using sunlight, so an oak tree is a producer.
Mushroom
A mushroom is a decomposer. It breaks down dead material.
Deer
A deer eats plants. It is a consumer.

SCI.q: In a food web, which way do the arrows point?
a: From the predator to the prey
This is backwards. Energy moves from the prey to the predator that eats it.
From the animal to the sun
The sun gives energy to producers. Energy doesn't flow back to the sun.
From bigger animals to smaller animals
Arrows show who eats whom, not size.
From the organism eaten to the organism that eats it
Arrows show the flow of energy, from the food to the eater.

SCI.q: A deer eats only plants. What kind of consumer is it?
a: Herbivore
Herbivores eat only plants, so a deer is a herbivore.
Carnivore
Carnivores eat only other animals.
Omnivore
Omnivores eat both plants and animals.
Decomposer
Decomposers break down dead things. A deer eats living plants.

SCI.q: Which part of a cell controls the cell's activities?
a: Cell membrane
The membrane controls what goes in and out of the cell, not all of its activities.
Cytoplasm
Cytoplasm is the jelly-like fluid that holds the cell parts.
Nucleus
The nucleus is the control center of the cell.
Cell wall
The cell wall gives plant cells support. Animal cells don't have one.

SCI.q: Which two body systems work together to get oxygen to every part of the body?
a: Skeletal and muscular
These systems work together to move the body, not to deliver oxygen.
Digestive and nervous
Digestion breaks down food, and nerves send signals. Neither one carries oxygen.
Respiratory and circulatory
The lungs take in oxygen, and the heart and blood carry it through the body.
Nervous and skeletal
These systems control and support the body. They don't move oxygen.

SCI.q: How do muscles help you bend your arm?
a: Muscles push on bones
Muscles can only pull. They contract, or shorten, and can't push.
Muscles pull on bones
Muscles contract and pull on bones to make them move.
Bones pull on muscles
Bones can't move by themselves. Muscles move them.
Nerves pull on bones
Nerves send the signal, but muscles do the pulling.

SCI.q: Which body system breaks food down into nutrients the body can use?
a: Circulatory system
The circulatory system carries nutrients around the body after food is broken down.
Skeletal system
The skeletal system supports and protects the body.
Respiratory system
The respiratory system takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.
Digestive system
The stomach and intestines break food down into nutrients.

SCI.q: You touch a hot stove and pull your hand away fast. Which system sent the message to move?
a: Nervous system
Nerves and the brain sense the heat and send a signal to your muscles.
Digestive system
The digestive system breaks down food. It doesn't sense heat.
Respiratory system
The respiratory system handles breathing, not reactions.
Skeletal system
Bones support your body, but they don't send signals.

SCI.q: A cold front is moving into central North Carolina. What weather should people most likely expect?
a: Clear skies for a week
Fronts bring changing weather, not a long calm stretch.
Thunderstorms, then cooler temperatures
A cold front pushes warm air up fast, which often causes storms. Then cooler air moves in.
Warmer, more humid air
That describes a warm front, not a cold front.
No change in the weather
When air masses meet at a front, the weather changes.

SCI.q: Water vapor rises, cools, and forms clouds. What is this step of the water cycle called?
a: Evaporation
Evaporation is liquid water turning into vapor. That happens before clouds form.
Precipitation
Precipitation is water falling as rain, snow, sleet, or hail.
Condensation
Condensation is water vapor cooling into tiny liquid drops, which form clouds.
Runoff
Runoff is water flowing over land into streams and rivers.

SCI.q: A barometer shows the air pressure is falling quickly. What does this usually mean?
a: Clear, sunny weather is coming
Rising pressure usually means clear weather.
Cloudy, stormy weather is likely
Falling air pressure usually means clouds and precipitation are on the way.
The temperature will stay the same
A barometer measures air pressure, not temperature.
It is about to get windless
Falling pressure often brings more wind, not less.

SCI.q: Which tool measures wind speed?
a: Thermometer
A thermometer measures temperature.
Rain gauge
A rain gauge measures how much rain falls.
Barometer
A barometer measures air pressure.
Anemometer
An anemometer has spinning cups that measure wind speed.

SCI.q: Tall, dark cumulonimbus clouds are building in the afternoon. What weather do they usually bring?
a: Thunderstorms
Cumulonimbus clouds are tall storm clouds that bring thunder, lightning, and heavy rain.
Clear skies
Clear skies have few or no clouds.
Light fog
Fog is a cloud that forms near the ground, not a tall storm cloud.
Fair weather all day
Puffy white cumulus clouds mean fair weather. Cumulonimbus clouds mean storms.

FR.q: Which fraction is equivalent to 1/2?
a: 2/3 is more than half. Half of 3 parts would be 1½ parts, not 2.
3/5 is more than half. Half of 5 parts would be 2½ parts.
1/2 × 4/4 = 4/8. Four out of eight equal parts is exactly half.
5/12 is less than half. Half of 12 is 6, so 6/12 would equal 1/2.

FR.q: 2/3 = ?/12. What number goes in the box?
a: This takes half of 12. Multiply instead: 3 × 4 = 12, so 2 × 4 = 8.
3 × 4 = 12, so multiply the numerator by 4 too: 2 × 4 = 8.
9/12 = 3/4, which is more than 2/3.
This adds 8 to the numerator. Use the same multiplier as the denominator.

FR.q: The top bar shows 3/4 shaded. The bottom bar is the same size but has 8 equal parts. How many parts should be shaded so both show the same amount?
a: 3/8 is less than 3/4, because eighths are smaller pieces than fourths.
4/8 is only half the bar. 3/4 is more than half.
7/8 is more than 3/4. One-fourth equals 2/8, so 3/4 = 6/8.

FR.q: Which fraction is NOT equivalent to 2/5?
a: 2/5 × 2/2 = 4/10, so this one is equivalent.
2/5 × 3/3 = 6/15, so this one is equivalent.
The numerator was multiplied by 2 but the denominator by 3. They must be multiplied by the same number, so 4/15 is NOT equivalent.
2/5 × 4/4 = 8/20, so this one is equivalent.

FR.q: Maria ate 6/10 of a pizza. Ty ate 3/5 of a pizza the same size. Who ate more?
a: Maria
6 is bigger than 3, but tenths are smaller pieces than fifths. The amounts are equal.
Ty
3/5 = 6/10, so Ty did not eat more.
They ate the same amount
3/5 × 2/2 = 6/10. Both ate the same amount.
There is not enough information
The pizzas are the same size, so you can compare the fractions.

FR.q: Which shows the correct way to make a fraction equivalent to 3/4?
a: Adding the same number changes the size of the fraction. 5/6 is more than 3/4.
Multiplying top and bottom by the same number makes smaller pieces but keeps the same amount.
Only the top was multiplied. 6/4 is more than one whole.
Only the bottom was multiplied. 3/8 is less than 3/4.

FR.q: Which fraction is equivalent to 9/12?
a: Divide the top and bottom by 3: 9 ÷ 3 = 3 and 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
Only the denominator changed. That doesn't make an equivalent fraction.
1/3 = 4/12, which is much less than 9/12.

FR.q: A point on a number line is at 2/6. Which fraction names the same point?
a: Divide the top and bottom by 2: 2/6 = 1/3. Both mark the same distance from 0.
2/3 = 4/6, twice as far from 0 as 2/6.
1/6 is only one sixth. 2/6 is two sixths.

FR.q: Which pair of fractions is equivalent?
a: 1 was added to the top and bottom. Adding doesn't make equivalent fractions.
The denominators are the same, but 2/5 has twice as many parts.

FR.q: 4/10 = ?/100. What number goes in the box?
a: 4/100 is much smaller than 4/10. The numerator must grow too.
10 was added to the numerator. Multiply by 10 instead.
The numerator was multiplied by 100, but the denominator only by 10.

FR.q: A recipe needs 1/4 cup of milk. Ana only has a 1/8 cup scoop. How many scoops does she need?
a: One scoop is only 1/8 cup, which is half of what she needs.
1/4 = 2/8, so she needs 2 scoops of 1/8 cup.
4 scoops = 4/8 cup = 1/2 cup. That's too much.
8 scoops = 8/8 = 1 whole cup. That's far too much.

FR.q: 3/? = 12/16. What number goes in the box?
a: 3/3 = 1 whole, but 12/16 is less than a whole.
3 × 4 = 12, so the denominator × 4 must be 16. 4 × 4 = 16, so 3/4 = 12/16.

FR.q: A rectangle is cut into 9 equal parts. How many parts must be shaded to show 2/3?
a: 2/9 uses the numerator without changing it. That is much less than 2/3.
5/9 is a little less than 2/3.

FR.q: Jamal says 2/3 = 4/5 because he added 2 to the top and bottom. Why is he wrong?
a: He should have added 3
Adding any number to the top and bottom changes the fraction's size.
Adding does not keep the fractions equal; he must multiply both by the same number
Multiplying top and bottom by the same number keeps the amount the same. Adding does not.
Fractions can never be equivalent
Many fractions are equivalent, like 1/2 and 2/4.
He should have subtracted 2
Subtracting also changes the size of the fraction.

FR.q: Which fraction is equivalent to 1 whole?
a: 1/8 is only one of eight parts.
7/8 is one part short of a whole.
When the numerator equals the denominator, every part is shaded. 8/8 = 1.
8/1 means 8 wholes, not 1.

FR.q: A garden has 12 rows. 8 rows are corn. Which fraction is equivalent to the part that is corn?
a: 1/2 = 6/12. The corn covers 8 rows, not 6.
Divide the top and bottom by 4: 8/12 = 2/3.
3/4 = 9/12, one row more than the corn.
Fifths don't divide 12 rows evenly, and 4/5 is not equal to 8/12.

FR.q: Which list shows fractions that are ALL equivalent to 1/3?
a: Each one is 1/3 times 2/2, 3/3, or 4/4.
These grow bigger each time. None equals 1/3.
Only the denominator changed, so each piece gets smaller.
These all equal 3 wholes, not 1/3.

FR.q: The bar shows 5/10 shaded. Which fraction is equivalent?
a: Divide the top and bottom by 5: 5/10 = 1/2. Half the bar is shaded.
5/5 is a whole bar, but only half is shaded.

FR.q: 3/8 = ?/24. What number goes in the box?
a: 6/24 = 2/8. Multiply 3 by 3, not by 2.
12/24 = 1/2, which is more than 3/8.
16 was added to the denominator. Multiply instead.

FR.q: Lena read 2/4 of her book. Max read 5/10 of the same book. Which statement is true?
a: Lena read more
2/4 = 1/2 and 5/10 = 1/2. Lena didn't read more.
Max read more
5 is bigger than 2, but tenths are smaller pieces. The amounts are equal.
They both read 1/2 of the book
2/4 = 1/2 and 5/10 = 1/2. They read the same amount.
They both read 1/4 of the book
Both fractions equal 1/2, not 1/4.

FR.q: 5/8 = ?/16. What number goes in the box?
a: 5/16 is half of 5/8. The numerator must be multiplied too.
8/16 = 1/2, which is less than 5/8.
8 was added to the numerator. Multiply by 2 instead.

FR.q: Which fraction is equivalent to 10/12?
a: Divide the top and bottom by 2: 10/12 = 5/6.

FR.q: 1/5 = ?/100. What number goes in the box?
a: 5/100 = 1/20, which is too small.
50/100 = 1/2, which is more than 1/5.
This subtracts 5 from 100. Multiply instead.

FR.q: Which number sentence is true?
a: 2 × 2 = 4 and 3 × 2 = 6, so these are equal.
2 was added to the top and bottom, which changes the amount.

FR.q: The top bar shows 4/6 shaded. The bottom bar is the same size with 3 equal parts. How many parts should be shaded so both show the same amount?
a: 1/3 = 2/6, half of what is shaded on top.
Divide the top and bottom by 2: 4/6 = 2/3.
3/3 is the whole bar, but the top bar isn't fully shaded.
There are only 3 parts in the bottom bar, so you can't shade 4.

FR.q: Ella says 3/6 and 4/8 are both equal to 1/2. Is she correct?
a: Yes, because 3 is half of 6 and 4 is half of 8
When the numerator is half the denominator, the fraction equals 1/2.
No, because 4/8 has bigger numbers
Bigger numbers don't mean a bigger amount. Eighths are smaller pieces than sixths.
No, because the denominators are different
Fractions with different denominators can still be equivalent.
Only 3/6 equals 1/2
4/8 also equals 1/2, because 4 is half of 8.

FR.q: 5/? = 15/18. What number goes in the box?
a: 5/3 is more than one whole, but 15/18 is less than one whole.
5/5 = 1 whole, but 15/18 is less than one whole.
5 × 3 = 15, so the denominator × 3 must be 18. 6 × 3 = 18.
10 was subtracted from 18. Divide by 3 instead.

FR.q: 8 out of 10 students brought a pencil. Which fraction is equivalent to 8/10?
a: Only the denominator changed. 8/5 is more than one whole.
Divide the top and bottom by 2: 8/10 = 4/5.

FR.q: Which shows how to prove that 2/5 = 6/15?
a: Adding fractions doesn't prove two fractions are equivalent.
Multiplying the top and bottom by 3 gives 6/15, so the fractions are equal.
Adding different numbers to the top and bottom doesn't keep the fraction the same.
Only the top was multiplied, which gives 6/5, not 6/15.

FR.q: Which fraction is equivalent to 3/12?
a: Divide the top and bottom by 3: 3/12 = 1/4.
3/4 = 9/12, three times as much.
1/12 is only one of twelve parts.
